beats.trigger: ## Security
beats.got: nothing new, a title

beats.trigger: You can't tell if your agent is safe from its output.
beats.got: Looking at what the agent writes won't tell me whether it is safe, so I need a separate check.

beats.trigger: Prework covers personal skills and agent risk layered on normal security.
beats.got: Three reading links, and I'm not sure I did them. I don't know what an agent trigger list is.

beats.trigger: **Apply** named agent risk patterns (direct and indirect prompt injection, secrets in context, tool confusion, skill supply chain) and a plain access review
beats.got: A list of jargon I'd have to ask about. 'Compliant, violating, can't tell' is something I understand.

beats.trigger: Name what you'd want to check before letting this near a real stakeholder.
beats.got: I'm asked to name my own worries first. That's a good question, and it's about my people's data.

beats.trigger: The harness turns that text into an action, and the tool does the work.
beats.got: Roughly, the agent writes text and something else turns it into actions. That is more technical than I wanted, and it never says who owns it.

beats.trigger: Would you bet your job on it being safe?
beats.got: There is no certainty here, and that applies to anything I would approve.

beats.trigger: Classical software security is a risk-based practice, and the software it protects is deterministic: same input, same output.
beats.got: Old security assumed software behaves the same way each time. That's a clear starting point.

beats.trigger: The dangerous move is getting your agent to *decide* to do something harmful with access it has, through well-formed English in a document it reads.
beats.got: An ordinary document can steer the agent, and nobody has to hack anything. That worries me for CVs and employee files.

beats.trigger: Scope (give the agent less). Split (two agents, different trust levels). Filter (post-process output). Gate (human approves). Review (a second agent judges).
beats.got: Five moves, and 'gate' means a person approves, which I can take to my HR partners.

beats.trigger: **"I can't tell"** is a real answer.
beats.got: I'm allowed to say 'I don't know yet' and have to write down the risk that remains, which is how leadership should handle it.

beats.trigger: More context makes a good answer likelier. Less access makes a bad answer smaller.
beats.got: After adding more all along, now I take access away, and that is a trade-off someone has to sign.

beats.trigger: Should the agent draft customer-facing language? If that is where the biggest risk lives, a human drafts and the agent reviews.
beats.got: Sometimes the safest design is that a person does the work. That sounds like a people decision, not an IT one.

beats.trigger: Damn, this is complex stuff.
beats.got: It's complex and it stays complex. The loop is the answer: read, pick, mitigate, name what's left, decide. A bit preachy.

beats.trigger: A **skill** packages an expertise (rules, checklists, the moves an agent runs) into something the agent loads when the work matches.
beats.got: A skill is a saved checklist the agent can reuse. I could do that for HR checks.

beats.trigger: Read the first few rows: they show which rules files can check and which need judgment, context, or a standing evidence check.
beats.got: Some rules a machine can check, and some still need a person.

beats.trigger: the customer your CEO would not want named in a transcript
beats.got: I tell it in plain words what matters for my company: employee data, works council, who must not be named. This part felt like mine.

beats.trigger: Expect many questions; the agent keeps probing both lenses over several rounds.
beats.got: It will quiz me for a long time. I can follow the policy lens. The agent-risk lens is more technical.

beats.trigger: *"You choose. Optimise for what I can't steer."*
beats.got: When I don't know, I can hand the choice back to the agent. That's a relief.

beats.trigger: Run `ls .claude/skills/agent-audit/` to confirm.
beats.got: A technical save step, with a command and a folder. I'd ask someone else to do it.

beats.trigger: Agent mitigations sit on top of normal company controls, not in place of them.
beats.got: The agent check adds to our existing controls and doesn't replace them, so legal and the DPO still matter.

beats.trigger: The goal is the loop (assess, mitigate, reassess residual), not a clean bill of health.
beats.got: I'm not looking for a pass. I'm practising the loop.

beats.trigger: Type `/` and look for `/agent-audit` in the autocomplete list.
beats.got: Check that the skill shows up. That's a technical step, and it's the second one in a row.

beats.trigger: Expect the reusable check to find things you did not think about, and to leave things "I can't tell" you thought were settled.
beats.got: The audit shows what I assumed was fine and wasn't. That is a report I could show someone.

beats.trigger: The uncomfortable feeling is the evidence.
beats.got: If the risks feel uncomfortable, that is the signal I need, and I should take it seriously.

beats.trigger: The risk remains. That is expected. Name it, accept it on record, and stop there.
beats.got: I fix one risk and write down the one that is left, with my name on it. That is how I'd want a manager to do it too.

beats.trigger: Bring the report, the files it quotes, the mitigation you applied, and the residual that remains.
beats.got: When I'm unsure I take the report to legal, the DPO or the works council. This is exactly what I was missing, a reason to go ask them.

beats.trigger: Risk control, done for every risk you found, separates a prototype from a production agent. You must do the work.
beats.got: One risk done is a prototype. Production needs all of them, and that is a lot of work.

beats.trigger: The reusable check is the expert in the room, and it carries to the next agent.
beats.got: The check can be reused for the next agent, and the report holds the decisions.

beats.trigger: The agent reviews the audit session and adds one to five rules to the root instructions file for future sessions.
beats.got: The agent writes rules for itself from what we found. I'm not sure who checks them.

beats.trigger: To share, give a teammate the skill and install it in their runtime.
beats.got: I could package how we review people data and give it to my HR partners. That's the spread from one person to a team that I care about.

beats.trigger: "I can't tell" is a real answer.
beats.got: Four points that repeat what I already took from the module.

beats.trigger: Without the two sentences, you'll be writing them while the rest of the room is already comparing detectors. Your call.
beats.got: Homework, with a mild nudge that I'll fall behind.

beats.trigger: What check was missing around the agent's output?
beats.got: Two real cases where nobody checked the output. I might read them.

take_homes: You can't judge whether an agent is safe by reading what it writes, so you build a repeatable check and run it, and 'I can't tell' is an acceptable result.
After a fix, write down the risk that remains and accept it on record, and when I can't judge it, take the report to legal, the DPO or the works council.
The safest mitigation is often giving the agent less access, or having a person do that part.

monday.move: Write the questions I'd put to our DPO and the works council about employee data in an AI tool, and bring the idea of a policy-check skill for HR to one HR partner.
monday.who: Me, then the DPO and one HR business partner
monday.when: Monday morning, before any agent touches HR data
monday.stop_condition: Stop at asking the questions and agreeing what data is off limits, without building anything before I have their answer.
monday.blocker: The works council and DPO haven't been asked yet, and I'm not technical enough to run the setup myself.

misconception.why: The module was about risk and never talked about roles or headcount. I still think headcount goes first and I still have no better answer for the leadership meeting. 'Give it less access, a person does that part' touches on it but doesn't answer it.

one_line: Good on how to think about risk and who to escalate to, but it never said what this means for my people, and the middle was too much command line.
